title.narrative: Improving Community Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (IC-WASH) in Kpatema, Kakuwa Chiefdom, Bo District

description.narrative:
This project intends to improve the health and well-being of 1,150 poor and vulnerable people of Kpaterna, Sierra Leone.
Sierra Leone remains one of the least developed nations in the world. Poverty is widespread and inequalities pervasive; gender discrimination poses a significant barrier to women and girls. In some cases, the situation is deteriorating, both at the local and national levels. Overall, 46% of the population in Sierra Leone has access to improved drinking water sources. Over half of the population in the south gets its water from unsafe sources.
Lack of access to safe water not only worsens rates of malnutrition, it is directly linked to child survival and impedes development efforts. Beyond immediate health risks, inadequate water supply and sanitation carry negative consequences for women and girls who shoulder the bulk of responsibility for collecting water.
The magnitude of demands for improved water sources in Kpatema community requires intensified efforts. Kpatema has long been excluded from previous WASH and other development interventions by NGOs. At present, Missionary Sisters of the Holy Rosary of the Bo Diocese is the only NGO implementing the Livelihood project in the community.
In Kpatema community, there are no safe water sources and no indication that the government or another NGO will address this problem with immediate urgency. The community members are continually forced to rely on unprotected wells, rivers, streams, and swamps for drinking water that are often contaminated. The problem is aggravated by the absence of latrines leading many communities to dispose of human waste into water sources.
Therefore the project aims to improve the health and well-being of 1,150 poor and vulnerable people of Kpatema community of Bo District through the provision of safe water, reliable sanitation, hygiene and sustainable water management. The WASH project will complement the child survival and development programme at UNICEF. It is hoped that this project’s interventions can improve knowledge, attitudes and practice in safe water, hygiene and sanitation at community level, including wider hand-washing campaigns.
